title: What AI is and what an agent is
description: What kind of program is really answering you, how an agent differs from a chat, and what parts it's made of.

steps.text: Before we go under the hood, let's agree on two words. You'll hear them in every lesson from here on: “model” and “agent.” Five minutes now will save a lot of confusion later.

steps.imagePrompt: Two scenes side by side: on the left, a talking chat bubble that only answers; on the right, the same chat bubble with small robot arms using a calendar, a phone and a toolbox.
steps.caption: A chat answers; an agent acts too

steps.question: You type a question and an answer comes back. What's on the other end? A program with canned answers, a search engine, a live person?
steps.answer: None of those. On the other end is a language model — a program trained to continue text. It doesn't keep ready-made answers and it doesn't search the internet: it picks which word comes next, and builds the answer piece by piece.

steps.definition: A program trained on an enormous amount of text. All it knows how to do is predict what comes next: which word is most likely to follow. An answer is built out of such predictions.
steps.example: You type “The capital of France is” and it continues with “Paris.” Not because it looked it up in a database, but because in the texts it was trained on, that word almost always came after a phrase like that.

steps.text: Three things follow from this right away, and the next few lessons are about them. It can be confidently wrong — to it, plausible and true are the same thing. It remembers nothing between answers. And on its own it only answers: it doesn't open files or set reminders.

The phrase “artificial intelligence” is misleading here: it makes it feel like someone inside is thinking and knows everything. What's inside is statistics over the texts it has read. That doesn't make the model useless, but it explains its quirks: why it makes things up, forgets, and asks you to clarify.
Now the second word. By itself, a model is just text in and text out. To make it useful in real life, you build scaffolding around it. A model with that scaffolding is already an agent.

steps.question: The app calls itself a pocket agent, and the course is called “Agent path.” How is this agent different from the chat we're talking in right now?
steps.answer: A chat answers in words. An agent also acts: it decides for itself what needs doing, and does it — checks the calendar, sets a reminder, creates an alarm. The difference isn't about being smarter, it's about being allowed to act.

steps.definition: A model that has been given three things: the freedom to choose its own next step, tools to carry that step out, and memory so it doesn't start from zero every time.
steps.example: You ask “what's up with my meeting tomorrow?” — a chat answers in generalities, an agent opens the calendar and tells you what's actually there.

steps.caption: Send the same request to the chat and to the agent — then look in “Alarms”

steps.text: What it's made of. The model is the engine: it decides what the next step is, but on its own it only writes text. Tools are the hands: that's how the agent acts. The loop is the order of work: it carries out what the model decided, hands the result back and calls the model again. Memory is how it remembers you between conversations. There's a lesson on each part ahead.

steps.instruction: What is each part of an agent responsible for?

pairs.def: decides what to do, but on its own only writes text
carries out the decision and gives the result back to the model

steps.text: And here's the answer to a question that would otherwise nag at you for half the course: why are the next lessons about tokens, temperature and hallucinations if the course is about agents? Because those are properties of the engine. Until you understand that the model sees only the text it's sent and remembers nothing, you can't understand why an agent needs memory and tools.

Practice. After the lesson, ask me in a regular chat to actually do something — for example, “set an alarm for 7:30.” Once I answer, a wrench icon appears in the chat header — “Show tools.” Tap it: in the “Tool calls” panel you can see that I didn't just answer, I called a tool. That's an agent at work.

In short. A language model is a program that predicts how text continues; that's where both its inventions and its forgetfulness come from. An agent is the same model, but with the freedom to choose its next step, plus tools and memory. It has four parts: the model decides, the tools act, the loop carries out the decision and returns the result, memory remembers. The next lessons are about the engine; after that, about the scaffolding around it.

options: A database of ready-made answers to common questions
A search engine that goes online for the answer
A program that predicts how a text continues
questions.explain: It doesn't store answers and it doesn't search: it picks the next word and builds the answer from those picks.

questions.q: Why can a model state something false with confidence?
options: It produces plausible text, not facts
It mixes things up on purpose to seem smarter
It takes its answers from an outdated internet
questions.explain: To it, plausible and true are the same thing: it predicts text rather than checking a database of facts.

questions.q: How is an agent different from an ordinary chat?
options: It answers noticeably faster and in more detail
It picks its own steps and acts with tools
It runs on a smarter, pricier model
questions.explain: It isn't about the model's brains but about permission to act: an agent can look at the calendar or set a reminder, not just answer in words.

questions.q: Which part of an agent can only write text?
questions.explain: The model is the engine: it generates text. Actions are carried out by tools.
